topics.ch: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read (with poem: Bharat Our Land)
topics.t: Sudha Murty's story: reading a first-person narrative
topics.h: Can a granddaughter become her grandmother's teacher? This lesson says yes, and it is told by the girl herself!
p: Sudha Murty is an Indian author who writes in both English and Kannada. In this lesson she recalls, in her own voice, teaching her grandmother to read.
A first-person narrative is told by a narrator who uses 'I' and 'me', so we see events through that person's eyes and feelings.
Every story has characters, a setting (time and place), a problem or conflict, and a resolution. The theme is the big idea the story leaves with us.
Stories about the past mostly use the simple past (she wrote). The past perfect (she had written) shows an action that happened before another past action.
Good readers infer: they use clues such as actions and descriptions to understand feelings that the writer does not state directly.

ex.q: Read this short passage (our own): 'Every evening Ajji sat on the swing with a slate on her lap. Her fingers, used to rolling rotis, now traced the curly letters of Kannada. When she finally read the name on the bus board aloud, she laughed like a child who had found a hidden sweet.' How does Ajji feel at the end, and which words show it?
st: Look at what Ajji does at the end: she reads the bus board aloud and laughs.
Look at the comparison: 'like a child who had found a hidden sweet' suggests surprise and delight.
Put the clues together to name the feeling.
ex.a: She feels joyful and proud; the words 'laughed like a child who had found a hidden sweet' show it.

topics.rl: When you help a younger cousin read a signboard or teach a grandparent to use a phone, you are living this story's theme.

topics.ch: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read (with poem: Bharat Our Land)
topics.t: Learning at any age: literacy words and modals
topics.h: Your nani learnt to use video calls, didn't she? Learning has no birthday limit!
p: Literacy is the ability to read and write. A literate person can read and write; an illiterate person cannot yet do so.
Words like literacy, literate, literal and literature belong to one word family. They come from the Latin word 'littera', meaning a letter of the alphabet.

Negative prefixes change a word to its opposite: il- before many words starting with l (illiterate, illegal), im- before many words starting with m or p (immature, impossible), ir- before many words starting with r (irregular).
Modals add meaning to verbs: can (present ability), could (past ability or a polite request), may (permission or possibility), must (necessity or a rule), should (advice).
Lifelong learning means continuing to learn throughout life, at any age.

ex.q: Fill in the modals: 'Last year Dadaji ___ not sign his name, but now he ___ write a whole letter.'
st: The first blank is about the past (last year) and ability, so we need the past form of 'can'.
The second blank is about ability now, so we need 'can'.
ex.a: could, can

topics.rl: International Literacy Day is observed every year on 8 September. Many villages and towns run evening classes where adults learn to read and write.

topics.ch: How I Taught My Grandmother to Read (with poem: Bharat Our Land)
topics.t: Poem on India's land: imagery and poetic devices
topics.h: Can a few lines of poetry fit the Himalayas, the sea and the desert all at once? Poets do it with clever word-pictures!
p: The lesson pairs the story with a poem on the theme of India's land. Poems like this often picture mountains, rivers, fields and seas.
Imagery is language that appeals to the senses: sight, sound, smell, taste or touch.
Personification gives human actions or feelings to non-human things, such as 'the river sings'.
A simile compares using 'like' or 'as'; a metaphor says one thing IS another. Alliteration repeats the same beginning consonant sound in nearby words.
The rhyme scheme is the pattern of rhyming line endings, marked with letters such as aabb or abab.

ex.q:
Read this original poem:
'From Himalayan peaks of snow
To southern seas where warm winds blow,
The Ganga hums a silver tune,
Thar's golden dunes sleep under the moon;
Green paddy dances in the rain,
One land, with colours none can contain.'
What is the rhyme scheme, and find one example of personification.
st: Mark the end words: snow, blow (a a); tune, moon (b b); rain, contain (c c).
Look for non-human things doing human actions: the Ganga hums, the dunes sleep, the paddy dances.
ex.a: The rhyme scheme is aabbcc; 'The Ganga hums a silver tune' is personification (so are 'dunes sleep' and 'paddy dances').

topics.rl: Patriotic songs sung on Republic Day and Independence Day are full of imagery of rivers, mountains and fields.

topics.ch: The Pot Maker (with poem: Gifts of Grace: Honouring Our Vocations)
topics.t: Craft and pottery: words from the potter's wheel
topics.h: A lump of mud, a spinning wheel and two patient hands: in minutes you have a diya! How does that magic happen?
p: The lesson 'The Pot Maker' is about the craft of pottery and the skill of the person who shapes clay.
Pottery is the craft of making pots and other objects from clay. A potter shapes wet clay on a spinning wheel, called a chaak in Hindi.
Key words: kiln (a very hot oven for firing clay), terracotta (baked clay; the Italian words mean 'baked earth'), glaze (a glassy coating), kulhad (a clay cup), matka (a clay water pot).
Clay is kneaded to make it smooth and to push out air bubbles, which could make a pot crack when it is fired.
To describe a process, we often use the passive voice: is/are + past participle, as in 'The clay is kneaded.' The action matters more than who does it.

ex.q: Change into the passive voice: 'The potter fires the pots in a kiln.'
st: Find the object of the active sentence: 'the pots'. It becomes the subject.
The verb 'fires' is in the simple present, so use are + past participle: 'are fired'.
Add 'by the potter' only if the doer is important.
ex.a: The pots are fired in a kiln (by the potter).

topics.rl: Kulhad chai at a railway station, matkas sold in summer and terracotta diyas at Diwali all come from a potter's wheel.

topics.ch: The Pot Maker (with poem: Gifts of Grace: Honouring Our Vocations)
topics.t: Dignity of work: respecting every vocation
topics.h: Who keeps your school clean, your clothes stitched and your shoes mended? Every one of them is a hero of everyday life!
p: Dignity of labour means that every kind of honest work deserves respect, whether it is done with the hands or with a pen.
Useful words: vocation (work a person feels suited to or called to do), artisan (a skilled craftsperson), livelihood (the way a person earns a living), toil (hard work).
Many job names are made by adding a suffix to a verb or noun: weave + er = weaver, sculpt + or = sculptor, art + ist = artist, electric + ian = electrician.
Subject-verb agreement: a singular subject takes a singular verb (The weaver works); two subjects joined by 'and' usually take a plural verb (The potter and his son work).
Words like each, every, everyone and nobody take a singular verb. With 'either ... or' and 'neither ... nor', the verb agrees with the subject nearer to it.

ex.q: Choose the correct verb: 'Every craftsperson in the village (take / takes) pride in good work.'
st: The subject begins with 'Every', which makes it singular.
A singular subject in the simple present takes the -s form of the verb.
ex.a: takes

topics.rl: On Labour Day (1 May) and on days like Teachers' Day, many schools thank the helpers, guards, cooks and cleaners who keep the school running.

topics.ch: The Pot Maker (with poem: Gifts of Grace: Honouring Our Vocations)
topics.t: Gifts of Grace: reading a poem about vocations
topics.h: The bread you eat, the shirt you wear, the book you read: count how many workers' gifts reach you before breakfast!
p: The poem in this lesson honours different vocations and the gifts each one brings to society.
The central idea of a poem is its main message, which can be said in one or two sentences.
Tone is the poet's attitude, such as grateful, joyful, sad or angry. Word choice shows the tone.
Anaphora is the repetition of the same word or words at the start of nearby lines, used for emphasis and rhythm.
A couplet is a pair of lines, usually rhyming; a quatrain is a stanza of four lines.

ex.q:
Read this original poem:
'The farmer gives the bread we break,
The weaver weaves the clothes we wear,
The teacher lights the minds awake,
The nurse brings comfort, calm and care.
No work is small, no hand is low;
Each gift of grace helps all to grow.'
What is the central idea and the tone?
st: Notice the list of workers and what each one gives us.
The last couplet sums it up: no work is small.
Words like 'gives', 'gift' and 'grace' show a thankful, respectful attitude.
ex.a: Central idea: every vocation is a gift that helps society, and no work is small. Tone: grateful and respectful.

topics.rl: Think of the dabbawalas of Mumbai, the farmers who grow your rice and the nurses in hospitals: every vocation is a gift to everyone.

topics.ch: Winds of Change (with poem: Canvas of Soil)
topics.t: Environment and change: words for a changing world
topics.h: A pond full of plastic turns into a pond full of lotuses. What changed? People did!
p: The lesson 'Winds of Change' is an article about the Indian hand fan (pankha) and how its use has changed over time. Here we take its big idea, change, and learn words for our changing environment.

Key words: conserve (protect and use carefully), sustainable (meeting today's needs without harming the future), deforestation (cutting down forests), renewable (able to be replaced naturally, like solar and wind energy), biodegradable (able to be broken down naturally by tiny living things).
Word families: pollute, pollution, pollutant; environment, environmental, environmentalist; sustain, sustainable, sustainability.
The present perfect (has/have + past participle) describes a change whose result we see now: 'The lake has become cleaner.' It is not used with finished time words such as 'yesterday' or 'last year'.
Cause and effect are linked with connectors such as because, so, as a result and therefore. 'Although' shows contrast.

ex.q: Read: 'Ten years ago the pond near Meena's school was choked with plastic. Then the students began a No-Plastic Tuesday drive. Now lotuses bloom there again and kingfishers have returned.' What caused the change, and which verb is in the present perfect?
st: Find what happened just before the pond improved: the students' drive against plastic.
Look for has/have + past participle: 'have returned'.
ex.a: The students' No-Plastic Tuesday drive caused the change; 'have returned' is in the present perfect.

topics.rl: Carrying a cloth bag to the market, using both sides of paper and switching off fans in an empty room are small changes that add up.

topics.ch: Winds of Change (with poem: Canvas of Soil)
topics.t: Farming and soil: words from the field
topics.h: Did you know a handful of healthy soil is home to millions of tiny living things? The soil is alive!
p: Farming words: sow (put seeds in the ground), irrigate (supply water to crops), harvest or reap (gather the ripe crop), fertile (able to grow good crops), barren (unable to grow crops), compost (rotted plant and food waste used to feed soil).
Homophones sound the same but differ in spelling and meaning: sow/sew, flour/flower, plain/plane, weather/whether.
In India, kharif crops such as rice, maize and cotton are sown with the start of the monsoon; rabi crops such as wheat, mustard and gram are sown in winter and harvested in spring.
Earthworms are called farmers' friends because they loosen the soil, let air and water in, and enrich it with their castings.
Alluvial soil, laid down by rivers, makes the northern plains very fertile; black soil holds moisture well and is especially good for cotton.

ex.q: Fill the homophones: 'Baba will ___ the seeds, and Ma will ___ the torn sack.'
st: The first blank is about seeds, so it needs the word meaning 'to plant': sow.
The second is about mending cloth with a needle: sew.
ex.a: sow, sew

topics.rl: Festivals such as Baisakhi, Pongal and Bihu are linked with harvest time, when families thank the land for its crops.

topics.ch: Winds of Change (with poem: Canvas of Soil)
topics.t: Canvas of Soil: metaphor and imagery in a farming poem
topics.h: What if a field were a painting and the farmer were the painter? Poets love that kind of 'what if'!
p: The poem's title, 'Canvas of Soil', pictures the soil as a canvas, like a painter's.
An extended metaphor carries one comparison across several lines, for example field = canvas, plough = brush, crops = colours.
Imagery of colour, touch and smell helps the reader feel the field: green shoots, golden wheat, cool damp earth.
Degrees of comparison: positive (bright), comparative (brighter), superlative (brightest). Poets use them to make pictures vivid.
A good descriptive paragraph uses sensory details and precise adjectives instead of vague words like 'nice'.

ex.q:
Read this original poem:
'The field is a canvas, bare and brown,
The plough, a brush, goes up and down;
With monsoon rain it paints in green,
The brightest shade you've ever seen.
In spring the wheat brings strokes of gold:
An artwork new, on earth so old.'
What is the extended metaphor here?
st: Line 1 calls the field a canvas.
Line 2 calls the plough a brush.
Lines 3 to 6 talk of painting, shades, strokes and an artwork, so the painting comparison continues.
ex.a: Farming is shown as painting: the field is the canvas, the plough is the brush, and the crops are the colours.

topics.rl: Look at a paddy field from a train window in the monsoon: the rows of bright green really do look like brushstrokes.

topics.ch: Vitamin-M (with poem: I Cannot Remember My Mother)
topics.t: Family and mothers: words of love and care
topics.h: Who remembers to pack your tiffin, even on the busiest morning? Families speak love in a hundred quiet ways.
p: The lesson 'Vitamin-M' is a family story about a boy, Ravi, and his grandfather, whose memory has grown weak. It shows that elders need patience, care and respect from their family, and its paired poem by Tagore remembers a mother.
Words of care: nurture (care for and help to grow), affection (fondness, gentle love), devotion (deep loyalty and love), cherish (hold dear), sacrifice (give up something for someone else).

Family phrasal verbs: bring up (raise a child), look after (take care of), take after (resemble an older family member), get along with (have a friendly relationship), look up to (admire and respect).
Idioms: 'the apple of someone's eye' means a person who is very dear; 'runs in the family' means a quality shared by many family members.
Writers often show love through actions rather than words. Readers infer feelings from what characters do.

ex.q: Read: 'Amma's alarm rings at five. By the time Ishaan wakes up, his tiffin is packed, his uniform ironed and a glass of warm haldi milk waits on the table. Amma only says, "Drink it before it gets cold." Ishaan smiles; he knows that is her way of saying "I love you."' How does Amma show her love?
st: Look at what Amma does: wakes early, packs the tiffin, irons the uniform, warms milk.
Look at what she says: only a simple reminder.
Ishaan's thought tells us her actions carry the message of love.
ex.a: She shows her love through caring actions rather than many words.

topics.rl: Next time someone in your family keeps the last piece of mithai for you, you'll know it is love in action!

topics.ch: Vitamin-M (with poem: I Cannot Remember My Mother)
topics.t: Talking in the family: reported speech
topics.h: Your little brother runs to you: 'Ma said you have to come home now!' He has just used reported speech!
p: Direct speech gives the exact words in quotation marks: Ma said, "I am tired." Reported (indirect) speech gives the meaning without quotation marks: Ma said that she was tired.
When the reporting verb is in the past, tenses usually move one step back: am/is → was, are → were, will → would, can → could, present perfect → past perfect.
Pronouns and time or place words change: today → that day, tomorrow → the next day, now → then, here → there. 'Said to' becomes 'told'.
Questions: yes/no questions use 'asked if/whether'; wh-questions keep the wh-word but use normal word order (asked where I was going).
Commands and requests use told/asked/requested + object + to + verb; a negative command uses 'not to'.

ex.q: Change into reported speech: Ma said to me, "I am making kheer today."
st: 'said to me' becomes 'told me'.
'I' (Ma) becomes 'she'; 'am making' moves back to 'was making'.
'today' becomes 'that day'.
ex.a: Ma told me that she was making kheer that day.

topics.rl: When you pass on a message from your teacher to your parents, you are using reported speech: 'Ma'am said that the PTM is on Saturday.'

topics.ch: Vitamin-M (with poem: I Cannot Remember My Mother)
topics.t: Tagore's poem on memory: senses and feelings
topics.h: Can a smell bring back a person? Catch a whiff of jasmine and suddenly you are in Nani's courtyard again!
p: Rabindranath Tagore (1861-1941) was a poet, writer, composer and painter from Bengal. In 1913 he won the Nobel Prize in Literature and became the first Asian to win a Nobel Prize.
Tagore wrote 'Jana Gana Mana', India's national anthem, and founded Visva-Bharati at Santiniketan.
In his poem 'I Cannot Remember My Mother', the speaker cannot clearly recall his mother, yet feels her presence in everyday sounds, scents and sights.
Memory poems often use sensory imagery and a nostalgic tone. Nostalgia is a warm, slightly sad longing for the past.
'Used to' + verb describes a past habit that no longer happens: 'Nani used to sing while she cooked.'

ex.q:
Read this original poem:
'I cannot see Nani's face so clear,
Yet when the evening kettle sings
Or jasmine scent drifts softly near,
I feel her close in little things.
Her lullabies still hum in rain;
She's far, yet always comes again.'
Which senses bring back the memory, and what is the tone?
st: 'the evening kettle sings' and 'lullabies' are sounds: hearing.
'jasmine scent' is a smell.
The speaker misses Nani but feels comforted, so the tone is tender and nostalgic.
ex.a: Hearing and smell bring back the memory; the tone is tender and nostalgic.

topics.rl: The smell of a particular agarbatti, the tune of an old film song or the taste of a festival sweet can bring back a loved one in a flash.

topics.ch: The World of Limitless Possibilities (with poem: Nine Gold Medals)
topics.t: Sports and inclusion: words that open doors
topics.h: What makes a game truly great: the fastest player, or the moment when everyone gets to play?
p: The lesson 'The World of Limitless Possibilities' is linked with sport and inclusion: people of all abilities taking part.

Key words: inclusion (making sure everyone is welcomed and can take part), accessible (easy for everyone, including people with disabilities, to reach and use), empathy (understanding and sharing another person's feelings), perseverance (continuing despite difficulty), resilience (the ability to bounce back).
Respectful, people-first language puts the person before the condition: 'a person with a disability', 'an athlete who uses a wheelchair'.
Prefixes make opposites: include/exclude, fair/unfair, able/unable, possible/impossible, accessible/inaccessible.
Adjectives describe nouns (a quick runner); adverbs usually describe verbs (she ran quickly). Many adverbs end in -ly.

ex.q: Read: 'When the class planned sports day, Kabir, who uses a wheelchair, expected to sit and watch. But his classmates added a wheelchair relay and a seated ball-throw. That evening Kabir wore a medal and the widest grin on the school bus.' How did the classmates show inclusion?
st: Notice Kabir's expectation: he thought he would only watch.
Notice what the classmates changed: they added events he could take part in.
The result: he took part and won a medal.
ex.a: They changed the events so that Kabir could take part, instead of leaving him out.

topics.rl: Ramps beside steps, audio announcements at railway stations and Braille on lift buttons all make places accessible.

topics.ch: The World of Limitless Possibilities (with poem: Nine Gold Medals)
topics.t: The Special Olympics spirit
topics.h: Imagine a sports meet where the loudest cheer is not for the fastest runner, but for the bravest try!
p: Special Olympics is a worldwide sports movement for people with intellectual disabilities. It was started by Eunice Kennedy Shriver, and the first International Special Olympics Summer Games were held in Chicago, USA, in 1968.
Its athlete oath is: 'Let me win. But if I cannot win, let me be brave in the attempt.' It values courage and effort over medals alone.
Athletes are grouped with others of similar ability so that every race is fair and everyone has a real chance. In India the movement is run by Special Olympics Bharat.
Unified Sports brings people with and without intellectual disabilities together as teammates.
Sports collocations are words that naturally go together: take part, break a record, win a medal, cross the finish line, cheer on.

ex.q: Think it through: What does 'let me be brave in the attempt' mean in the athlete oath?
st: 'Attempt' means a try or an effort.
The oath first hopes for a win, then says what matters if winning is not possible.
So it asks for courage while trying, whatever the result.
ex.a: It means that even if I don't win, I want to try with courage and give my best effort.

topics.rl: Many Indian schools hold inclusive sports days and Unified Sports matches where children of all abilities play on the same team.

topics.ch: The World of Limitless Possibilities (with poem: Nine Gold Medals)
topics.t: Nine Gold Medals: a story told in a poem
topics.h: A poem that tells a whole story, with a twist at the end? That's a narrative poem, and you're about to read one!
p: 'Nine Gold Medals' is a narrative poem about athletes in a race who choose kindness over winning.
A narrative poem tells a story with characters, a setting, events, a climax (the turning point) and an ending.
A paradox is a statement that seems to contradict itself but holds a deeper truth, for example 'We lost, yet we won'.
Stories in verse usually use the simple past: ran, fell, knelt, cheered.
A good summary gives only the main events in your own words and in the right order, and is much shorter than the original.

ex.q:
Read this original narrative poem:
'Our team was one point from the cup
When Meenu's shoelace tangled up;
The rival captain paused the play
And knelt to help her on her way.
We lost the match, the scoreboard said,
But all of us walked home ahead.'
What is the climax, and what is the message?
st: The tension builds: the team is one point from winning.
The turning point is when the rival captain stops the play to help Meenu.
The last two lines say they lost on the scoreboard but felt like winners.
ex.a: The climax is the rival captain pausing the play to help Meenu. The message: kindness and sportsmanship matter more than the score.

topics.rl: Think of a time a player in a cricket or football match helped an injured opponent; the crowd often claps more for that than for a goal.

topics.ch: Twin Melodies (with poem: A Friend Found in Music)
topics.t: Music: words of rhythm and melody
topics.h: A tabla, a flute and a power cut: that's all it takes to turn a dark corridor into a concert!
p: The lesson 'Twin Melodies' is a play about Shruti, a young violinist who plays fusion music with her band, and her father, who loves traditional music. Music is at its heart, and the paired poem shows music as a friend.
Music words: melody (a tune), rhythm (a pattern of beats), tempo (the speed of music), lyrics (the words of a song), harmony (different notes sounding pleasant together).
Indian classical music has two main traditions: Hindustani, mainly in North India, and Carnatic, mainly in South India. A raga is a melodic framework; a tala is a rhythmic cycle.
Instruments can be grouped as string (sitar, veena, sarod), wind (bansuri, shehnai, nadaswaram) and percussion (tabla, mridangam, dholak).

Great Indian musicians: Ustad Bismillah Khan (shehnai), Pandit Ravi Shankar (sitar), Ustad Zakir Hussain (tabla), Pandit Hariprasad Chaurasia (bansuri) and M. S. Subbulakshmi (Carnatic vocal), the first musician to receive the Bharat Ratna.

ex.q: Fill the gaps: 'The tabla kept a steady ___ while the sitar played a sweet ___.'
st: A tabla is a drum, so it gives the beat: rhythm.
A sitar plays a tune: melody.
ex.a: rhythm, melody

topics.rl: From wedding bands to school assembly songs and festival bhajans, music is everywhere in Indian life.

topics.ch: Twin Melodies (with poem: A Friend Found in Music)
topics.t: Friendship: idioms, phrasal verbs and relative clauses
topics.h: Who is the friend you'd call first with good news? Friendship has its own special vocabulary!
p: Friendship words: companion (someone you spend time with), confidant (a person you trust with secrets), loyal (faithful), trustworthy (can be relied on), inseparable (always together).
Phrasal verbs: stand by (support), count on (rely on), fall out (quarrel), make up (become friends again after a quarrel), drift apart (slowly become less close).

Idioms: 'a friend in need is a friend indeed' (a true friend helps when you need it), 'thick as thieves' (very close), 'see eye to eye' (agree), 'break the ice' (start a friendly conversation in an awkward moment).
Relative pronouns join ideas: who for people (a friend who listens), which for things (the song which we sang), whose for possession (the boy whose sister sings).

ex.q: Choose the relative pronoun: 'Ananya is the friend ___ always shares her lunch with me.'
st: The word before the gap is 'friend', a person.
The gap is the subject of 'shares', and for people we use 'who'.
ex.a: who

topics.rl: Making a new friend on the first day of school, standing by a friend during exams or making up after a fight: friendship is daily practice!

topics.ch: Twin Melodies (with poem: A Friend Found in Music)
topics.t: A Friend Found in Music: sound devices in poetry
topics.h: Have you ever felt that a song understood you better than anyone? Poets call that a friendship too!
p: The poem in this lesson presents music as a companion that comforts and stays with us.

Sound devices make poems musical: rhyme (matching end sounds), rhythm (a pattern of beats), alliteration (repeated beginning consonant sounds), assonance (repeated vowel sounds inside nearby words, as in 'sweet green leaves') and onomatopoeia (words that imitate sounds, like jingle or dhum).
A refrain is a line or group of lines repeated in a poem or song, like a chorus.
Personification lets music act like a person: it can whisper, hug or hold your hand.
'Feeling blue' is an idiom meaning feeling sad.

ex.q:
Read this original poem:
'When I am lonely, music comes
And taps my shoulder with its drums;
The flute-notes whisper, "Don't be blue,"
The sitar strums, "I'm here for you."
Dha-dhin, the tabla keeps the beat,
A friend that lifts my dancing feet.'
Find one example each of personification and onomatopoeia.
st: Music 'comes', 'taps my shoulder' and the flute-notes 'whisper': these are human actions.
'Dha-dhin' imitates the sound of the tabla.
ex.a: Personification: 'music comes / And taps my shoulder' (also 'flute-notes whisper'). Onomatopoeia: 'Dha-dhin'.

topics.rl: Many people play their favourite songs when they are tired or sad; music can feel like a friend who always understands.

topics.ch: Carrier of Words (with poem: Words)
topics.t: Communication: getting the message across
topics.h: A wink, a postcard, a voice note and a namaste: four very different ways to say something!
p: The lesson 'Carrier of Words' is about communication, that is, how messages travel from one person to another.
Verbal communication uses words, spoken or written. Non-verbal communication uses gestures, facial expressions, body language and tone of voice.
Formal language suits officials and people we don't know well: full sentences, polite requests, no slang. Informal language suits friends and family and may use contractions like I'm and can't.
A formal letter has: sender's address, date, receiver's address, subject, salutation (Sir/Madam), body, complimentary close (Yours faithfully), and signature with name.
In India, the six-digit PIN code (Postal Index Number) helps the postal service deliver letters to the right area.

ex.q: Which line suits a leave application to the principal? (a) 'Hey, can I skip school on Monday?' (b) 'I request you to kindly grant me leave for two days.'
st: A principal is addressed formally, so slang like 'Hey' and 'skip' is not suitable.
Line (b) is a polite, complete request using formal words like 'request' and 'kindly grant'.
ex.a: Line (b), because it is formal and polite.

topics.rl: Writing a leave application, sending a festival message to your cousin and giving directions to a visitor all need different styles of communication.

topics.ch: Carrier of Words (with poem: Words)
topics.t: The power of words: shades of meaning
topics.h: 'Slim' or 'skinny'? 'Curious' or 'nosy'? One small word choice can make someone smile or frown!
p: Words can hurt or heal, so we choose them with care. 'Think before you speak' is good advice.
Denotation is a word's dictionary meaning. Connotation is the feeling a word carries: 'thrifty' sounds positive, 'stingy' sounds negative, though both describe careful spending.
Polite words and phrases (please, could you, thank you, I'm sorry) make requests and disagreements kinder.
Tricky homophones: its (belonging to it) / it's (it is); your (belonging to you) / you're (you are); their (belonging to them) / there (a place) / they're (they are).
The saying 'The pen is mightier than the sword' means ideas and words can have more power than force.

ex.q: Which feedback on a friend's drawing is kinder and more useful? (a) 'Your drawing is bad.' (b) 'I love the colours; maybe the trees could be a little bigger?'
st: (a) only judges and gives no help.
(b) praises something real and gives a gentle, specific suggestion.
ex.a: (b), because it is kind and gives a clear suggestion for improvement.

topics.rl: Saying 'Could you please pass the chutney?' instead of 'Give the chutney!' at the dinner table is the power of words in action.

topics.ch: Carrier of Words (with poem: Words)
topics.t: Words: a poem about words, and parts of speech
topics.h: A single word can be a noun at breakfast and a verb by lunch. Words are shape-shifters!
p: The poem 'Words' in this lesson is about the power of words.
Metaphors help poets show the power of words: words as seeds, thorns or wings.
English has eight parts of speech: noun, pronoun, verb, adjective, adverb, preposition, conjunction and interjection.
The same word can be a different part of speech in different sentences: 'Switch on the light' (noun), 'Light the diya' (verb), 'a light bag' (adjective).
Conjunctions (and, but, because) join words or clauses; prepositions (in, on, under) show how a noun relates to other words; interjections (Wow! Oh!) express sudden feeling.

ex.q:
Read this original poem:
'Words are seeds we gently sow,
In other hearts they root and grow;
A harsh word is a thorn that stings,
A kind word gives the spirit wings.
So weigh each word before it flies:
Once spoken, no word ever dies.'
What is the poem's message, and name one metaphor.
st: Lines 1 to 4 show words growing in hearts, stinging or lifting people.
Lines 5 and 6 advise us to think before we speak because words last.
'Words are seeds' says words ARE seeds, without 'like' or 'as'.
ex.a: Message: words have lasting power, so think before you speak. Metaphor: 'Words are seeds' (also 'A harsh word is a thorn').

topics.rl: A kind message to a friend before an exam can stay with them for years; so can a mean comment. That's why we weigh our words.

topics.ch: Follow That Dream (with poem: Believe in Yourself)
topics.t: Ambition: dreams, goals and talking about the future
topics.h: Every big dream starts as a tiny 'what if'. What if you are the next great scientist, singer or athlete?
p: The lesson 'Follow That Dream' is about ambition: having a goal and working steadily towards it.

Key words: ambition (a strong wish to achieve something), aspire (to hope and work to achieve something), goal, obstacle (something in the way), persevere (keep going despite difficulty), milestone (an important stage of progress).
Talking about the future: 'will' for predictions and on-the-spot decisions; 'be going to' for plans and for things we can see coming ('Look at those clouds; it is going to rain').
The present continuous can show fixed arrangements ('I am meeting my coach tomorrow'); the simple present is used for timetables ('The train leaves at 6:10').
Big dreams become real through small, steady steps.

ex.q: Choose the right future form: 'Look at those dark clouds! It ___ rain.'
st: We can see evidence now: dark clouds.
When present evidence shows something is about to happen, we use 'be going to'.
ex.a: is going to

topics.rl: Dr A. P. J. Abdul Kalam grew up in Rameswaram and sold newspapers as a boy before becoming a scientist and President of India. Kalpana Chawla became the first woman of Indian origin to go to space.

topics.ch: Follow That Dream (with poem: Believe in Yourself)
topics.t: Self-belief: idioms and contrast words
topics.h: What do you say to yourself just before an exam? Those quiet words might be the most important ones of the day!
p: Self-belief is confidence in your own abilities. Self-doubt is its opposite. An optimistic person expects good things; a pessimistic person expects the worst.
Idioms: 'keep your chin up' (stay cheerful in hard times), 'rise to the occasion' (do well when it really matters), 'never say die' (never give up), 'against all odds' (despite great difficulties).
Positive self-talk turns 'I can't do this' into 'I can't do this yet, but I'm learning.'

Contrast words: 'although' and 'even though' are followed by a clause (Although she was nervous, she sang). 'Despite' and 'in spite of' are followed by a noun or an -ing form (Despite her nerves, she sang). We never say 'despite of'.

ex.q: Join the two sentences using 'although': 'She was nervous. She sang beautifully.'
st: 'Although' introduces the contrasting idea, which has a subject and a verb: she was nervous.
Add a comma, then the main clause.
ex.a: Although she was nervous, she sang beautifully.

topics.rl: Before a match, a speech or a board exam, many people take a deep breath and remind themselves how much they have prepared.

topics.ch: Follow That Dream (with poem: Believe in Yourself)
topics.t: Believe in Yourself: imperatives, sentence types and diary writing
topics.h: 'Stand up! Try again! Believe!' Notice anything? Poems of courage love command words!
p: The poem 'Believe in Yourself' in this lesson encourages the reader to trust their own strength and keep going.
Imperative sentences give commands, advice or encouragement. They start with the base form of a verb, and the subject 'you' is understood: 'Stand firm.'
The four types of sentences are declarative (statement), interrogative (question), imperative (command or request) and exclamatory (strong feeling, often with What or How and an exclamation mark).
Repeating a word at the start of lines (anaphora) and making storms or doubts speak (personification) add force to a poem.
A diary entry has the date, day and time, is written in the first person, records events and feelings in an informal style, and ends with your name.

ex.q:
Read this original poem:
'Believe the seed that dreams of tree,
Believe the stream that seeks the sea;
When storms say "Stop!" and doubts say "No,"
Stand up, stand firm, and still say "Go!"
The sky is not your ceiling, friend:
It's just the start, it's not the end.'
Find an imperative and explain 'The sky is not your ceiling'.
st: 'Stand up, stand firm' begins with base verbs and gives encouragement: imperative.
A ceiling stops you from going higher; the poet says the sky is not such a limit.
So the line means there is no fixed limit to how far you can rise.
ex.a: Imperative: 'Stand up, stand firm'. 'The sky is not your ceiling' means there is no limit to what you can achieve.

topics.rl: Keeping a diary of your goals and small wins, like finishing a chapter or a tough practice session, is a great way to build self-belief.

qa.q: 'I watched my grandmother press her thumb on the ink pad, her eyes lowered.' From which point of view is this sentence told?
qa.e: The narrator uses 'I', so the sentence is told in the first person.

qa.q: Which sentence uses the past perfect tense correctly?
qa.a: She had learnt the letters before the festival began.
qa.e: The past perfect is had + past participle (had learnt). It shows the learning was finished before another past action (the festival began).

qa.q: In a story, what does the 'setting' mean?
qa.a: The time and place where the story happens
qa.e: The setting tells us when and where events take place.

qa.q: Read: 'Rehana's grandfather hid the letter behind his back whenever the postman came, then quietly asked the neighbour's boy to read it to him.' What can you infer?
qa.a: He cannot read and feels shy about it
qa.e: Asking someone else to read the letter and hiding it suggests he cannot read and is embarrassed about it.

qa.q: Which word best describes a learner who keeps trying even when lessons are hard?
qa.e: 'Determined' means firmly deciding to do something and not giving up.

qa.q: Which statement best describes the theme of a story?
qa.a: The central idea or message it shares
qa.e: The theme is the main idea or insight about life that the story conveys.

qa.q: In which languages does Sudha Murty write?
qa.e: Sudha Murty writes in both English and Kannada, the language of Karnataka.

qa.q: Choose the correct verb: 'Yesterday, Ajji ___ her name for the first time.'
qa.e: 'Yesterday' points to a finished past time, so we use the simple past 'wrote'.

qa.q: What is the opposite of 'literate'?
qa.e: Words beginning with 'l' often take the prefix il-, so literate becomes illiterate.

qa.q: Which word does NOT come from the Latin 'littera' (letter)?
qa.e: 'Liberty' comes from a different Latin word meaning free; the others are linked to letters.

qa.q: What does 'lifelong' mean in 'lifelong learning'?
qa.e: 'Lifelong' means continuing for the whole of a person's life.

qa.q: 'You should read for twenty minutes every day.' What does 'should' express here?
qa.e: 'Should' is used to give advice or a suggestion.

qa.q: Read: 'At sixty-five, Kamla Bai joined the evening class at the panchayat hall. At first her hand shook as she held the chalk. By Diwali she could write the names of all her grandchildren.' What change happened in Kamla Bai?
qa.e: The passage says that by Diwali she could write her grandchildren's names, so she learnt to write.

qa.q: Which prefix makes the opposite of 'responsible'?
qa.e: Many words beginning with 'r' take ir-, giving 'irresponsible'.

qa.q: In which sentence does 'could' show past ability?
qa.a: As a girl, Nani could climb the mango tree in seconds.
qa.e: 'As a girl' places the action in the past, and 'could' tells what she was able to do then.

qa.q: Which saying best matches the idea that learning has no age limit?
qa.a: It is never too late to learn.
qa.e: 'It is never too late to learn' says anyone can start learning at any age.

qa.q: 'Thar's golden dunes sleep under the moon.' Which device is used here?
qa.e: Sand dunes cannot sleep; giving them a human action is personification.

qa.q: What is the rhyme scheme of these lines? 'The mountains stand so proud and tall, / They guard the land, they watch us all. / The rivers run to meet the sea, / And sing of home to you and me.'
qa.e: tall/all rhyme (aa) and sea/me rhyme (bb), giving aabb.

qa.q: Which line contains a simile?
qa.a: Her smile was as bright as a diya.
qa.e: It compares her smile to a diya using 'as ... as', which makes it a simile.

qa.q: 'The smell of wet earth after the first rain' appeals mainly to which sense?
qa.e: The word 'smell' tells us the image appeals to the sense of smell.

qa.q: 'India is a necklace of many bright beads.' Which device is this?
qa.e: It says India IS a necklace, without 'like' or 'as', so it is a metaphor.

qa.q: Which word describes the Himalayas most vividly in a poem?
qa.e: 'Majestic' means grand and impressive, which suits huge snowy mountains.

qa.q: What does 'diverse' mean in 'India is a diverse land'?
qa.e: 'Diverse' means varied, with many different kinds of people, places and cultures.

qa.q: Which pair of words rhymes?
qa.e: 'Tune' and 'moon' end with the same 'oon' sound.

qa.q: What is a kiln?
qa.a: A very hot oven used to fire clay objects
qa.e: A kiln is an oven or furnace that heats clay to a high temperature so that it hardens.

qa.q: What does the word 'terracotta' literally mean?
qa.e: 'Terracotta' comes from Italian words meaning 'baked earth'.

qa.q: Which is the correct passive form of 'The potter shapes the clay'?
qa.a: The clay is shaped by the potter.
qa.e: The object 'the clay' becomes the subject, and the simple present passive is is + past participle (is shaped).

qa.q: Why does a potter knead the clay before shaping it?
qa.a: To make it smooth and push out air bubbles
qa.e: Kneading makes the clay even and removes trapped air that could cause cracks in the kiln.

qa.q: Read: 'In Ramu Kaka's courtyard the wheel spun with a soft whirr. A lump of grey clay rose between his palms, and in a minute it had become a little lamp. "Clay listens to patient hands," he smiled.' What does Ramu Kaka mean?
qa.a: Good work in clay needs patience
qa.e: He means clay takes a good shape only when the potter works calmly and patiently.

qa.q: 'A lump of clay rose between his palms like a growing bud.' Which device is used?
qa.e: The clay is compared to a bud using 'like', so it is a simile.

qa.q: Which sentence is in the passive voice?
qa.a: Diyas are made in large numbers before Diwali.
qa.e: 'Are made' is be + past participle, and the subject (diyas) receives the action.

qa.q: Why does water in a clay matka stay cool in summer?
qa.a: Water seeps through tiny pores and evaporates, cooling the pot
qa.e: A matka has tiny pores; water slowly seeps out and evaporates from the surface, and evaporation cools the pot and the water.

qa.q: What does 'dignity of labour' mean?
qa.a: Every kind of honest work deserves respect
qa.e: Dignity of labour is the idea that all honest work, of hand or mind, is worthy of respect.

qa.q: What does 'livelihood' mean?
qa.a: The way a person earns a living
qa.e: Livelihood is the means by which a person earns money to live.

qa.q: Which word is a synonym of 'artisan'?
qa.e: An artisan is a skilled worker who makes things by hand, that is, a craftsperson.

qa.q: Choose the correct verb: 'The potter and his daughter ___ pots at the fair every Sunday.'
qa.e: Two subjects joined by 'and' make a plural subject, so the verb is 'sell'.

qa.q: Choose the correct verb: 'Neither the baskets nor the mat ___ ready yet.'
qa.e: With 'neither ... nor', the verb agrees with the nearer subject, 'the mat', which is singular.

qa.q: Which is the correct word for a person who sculpts?
qa.e: The job name is 'sculptor', with the suffix -or.

qa.q: Read: 'Lakshmi Didi sweeps the school corridor before the first bell. When Arjun dropped his lunch, she helped him clean up with a smile. On Teachers' Day the class gave her a card that said, "Our school shines because of you."' What does the card show?
qa.a: The class respects and values her work
qa.e: The card thanks her and says the school shines because of her, which shows respect and gratitude.

qa.q: What is the antonym of 'respect'?
qa.e: Adding dis- gives the opposite meaning: disrespect.

qa.q: 'No work is small, no hand is low; / Each gift of grace helps all to grow.' What is the central idea of these lines?
qa.a: Every kind of work has value and helps everyone
qa.e: The lines say no work is small and every 'gift' of work helps all of us grow.

qa.q: 'Thank you, hands that sow the grain, / Thank you, hands that mend the drain.' What is the tone?
qa.e: The repeated 'Thank you' shows a grateful tone.

qa.q: What is the repetition of the same word at the start of nearby lines called?
qa.e: Anaphora is repeating a word or phrase at the beginning of successive lines.

qa.q: In the line 'No hand is low', what does 'hand' stand for?
qa.e: Here 'hand' stands for a person who works, as in 'farmhand'.

qa.q: 'The weaver weaves the clothes we wear.' What is the subject of this sentence?
qa.e: The subject is who does the action: the weaver weaves.

qa.q: What does 'vocation' mean?
qa.a: Work a person feels especially suited to
qa.e: A vocation is a job or calling that a person feels drawn to and suited for.

qa.q: Which word is a synonym of 'honour' when used as a verb?
qa.e: To honour someone is to respect them and show it.

qa.q: A stanza of two lines that usually rhyme is called a:
qa.e: A couplet is a pair of lines, usually rhyming.

qa.q: What does 'sustainable' mean?
qa.a: Meeting present needs without harming the future
qa.e: Sustainable living meets our needs today while protecting resources for the future.

qa.q: Which of these is biodegradable?
qa.e: A banana leaf is natural material that tiny organisms break down in a short time.

qa.q: Which sentence uses the present perfect correctly?
qa.a: Many birds have returned to the lake this winter.
qa.e: 'Have returned' is have + past participle, and 'this winter' is a time that is not yet over.

qa.q: What is the noun form of the verb 'pollute'?
qa.e: Adding -ion to 'pollute' gives the noun 'pollution'.

qa.q: What is the antonym of 'conserve'?
qa.e: To conserve is to use carefully; to waste is the opposite.

qa.q: Read: 'When the hills above the village lost their trees, the rains washed the soil down into the stream. The water turned muddy and the fields below flooded more often.' What made the stream muddy?
qa.a: Soil washed down from the bare hills
qa.e: Without trees to hold it, the soil was washed into the stream by the rain.

qa.q: Which of these is a renewable source of energy?
qa.e: The Sun's energy is replaced naturally every day, so it is renewable.

qa.q: The phrase 'winds of change' is used to mean:
qa.e: 'Winds of change' is an expression for influences or forces that bring change.

qa.q: What is fertile soil?
qa.a: Soil that can grow plenty of good crops
qa.e: Fertile soil is rich in nutrients and grows good crops.

qa.q: Which word is the antonym of 'fertile'?
qa.e: Barren land cannot grow crops, the opposite of fertile.

qa.q: Choose the correct homophone: 'Dadi ground the wheat into fine ___.'
qa.e: 'Flour' is powder made by grinding grain; a 'flower' is the bloom of a plant.

qa.q: Which of these is a rabi crop?
qa.e: Wheat is sown in winter and harvested in spring, so it is a rabi crop.

qa.q: Why are earthworms called farmers' friends?
qa.a: They loosen the soil and make it richer
qa.e: Earthworms dig tunnels that let air and water in, and their castings add nutrients.

qa.q: What does 'irrigate' mean?
qa.a: To supply water to land or crops
qa.e: To irrigate is to bring water to fields, for example through canals, wells or drip pipes.

qa.q: Read: 'Kavya's grandfather never burns the leftover stalks after harvest. He ploughs them back into the field and spreads compost. "Feed the soil, and the soil will feed you," he says.' What does he mean?
qa.a: Caring for the soil gives good crops in return
qa.e: He means that if we keep the soil healthy, it will give us good harvests.

qa.q: Which crop grows especially well in black soil?
qa.e: Black soil holds moisture well and is famous for cotton, which is why it is also called black cotton soil.

qa.q: 'The field is a canvas, bare and brown.' What is the field compared to?
qa.e: The line directly says the field is a canvas, which is a metaphor.

qa.q: What is an extended metaphor?
qa.a: A metaphor that is continued over several lines
qa.e: An extended metaphor develops one comparison through many lines or a whole poem.

qa.q: In 'With monsoon rain it paints in green', what does the green stand for?
qa.a: Young crops growing after the rain
qa.e: After the monsoon rain, young crops cover the field in green.

qa.q: What is the rhyme scheme of these lines? 'The field is a canvas, bare and brown, / The plough, a brush, goes up and down; / With monsoon rain it paints in green, / The brightest shade you've ever seen.'
qa.e: brown/down rhyme (aa) and green/seen rhyme (bb).

qa.q: Which phrase appeals to the sense of touch?
qa.a: The cool, damp soil between my toes
qa.e: 'Cool' and 'damp' describe how something feels on the skin.

qa.q: 'An artwork new, on earth so old.' What attitude does the poet show towards farming?
qa.e: Calling farming an 'artwork' shows that the poet admires it.

qa.q: In 'The brightest shade you've ever seen', which degree of comparison is 'brightest'?
qa.e: 'Brightest' (-est) compares one thing with all others, so it is superlative.

qa.q: Which sentence is the most vivid description of a field?
qa.a: Rows of tender green paddy shivered in the wet breeze.
qa.e: It uses precise adjectives and sensory details (tender, green, shivered, wet breeze).

qa.q: What does 'nurture' mean?
qa.a: To care for and help to grow
qa.e: To nurture is to look after someone or something and help it develop.

qa.q: What does 'look after' mean in 'Didi looks after our baby brother'?
qa.e: 'Look after' means to take care of someone.

qa.q: 'Meera looks up to her mother.' What does this mean?
qa.a: Meera admires and respects her mother
qa.e: To look up to someone is to admire and respect them.

qa.q: Read: 'Papa never says much, but every night he quietly covers Tara with a blanket after she falls asleep.' What can you infer about Papa?
qa.e: His quiet nightly action shows care, even without words.

qa.q: Which word is a synonym of 'affection'?
qa.e: Affection is a gentle feeling of love, which is fondness.

qa.q: What does 'the apple of someone's eye' mean?
qa.a: A person who is very dear to someone
qa.e: The idiom describes a person someone loves and treasures greatly.

qa.q: Which sentence uses the apostrophe correctly?
qa.e: For one mother, the possessive is mother + 's: mother's.

qa.q: What is the antonym of 'cherish'?
qa.e: To cherish is to hold dear; to neglect is to fail to care for.

qa.q: Choose the reported form: Ma said, "I am tired."
qa.a: Ma said that she was tired.
qa.e: 'I' becomes 'she' and 'am' moves back to 'was'. 'Said' with no listener stays 'said'.

qa.q: Choose the reported form: Papa said to me, "Close the door."
qa.a: Papa told me to close the door.
qa.e: A command becomes told + object + to + verb.

qa.q: Choose the reported form: Dadi said to me, "Have you eaten lunch?"
qa.a: Dadi asked me if I had eaten lunch.
qa.e: A yes/no question uses 'asked if', normal word order, and the present perfect moves back to the past perfect.

qa.q: Choose the reported form: Didi said to me, "Where are you going?"
qa.a: Didi asked me where I was going.
qa.e: Keep 'where', use normal order (I was going) and move the tense back.

qa.q: Choose the reported form: Mother said to Riya, "Don't touch the hot pan."
qa.a: Mother told Riya not to touch the hot pan.
qa.e: A negative command becomes told + object + not to + verb.

qa.q: In reported speech, what does 'tomorrow' usually become?
qa.e: When reporting later, 'tomorrow' becomes 'the next day' or 'the following day'.

qa.q: Choose the reported form: Ravi said, "I will help Ma."
qa.a: Ravi said that he would help Ma.
qa.e: 'I' becomes 'he' and 'will' moves back to 'would'.

qa.q: Choose the reported form: Nana said to me, "Please pass the salt."
qa.a: Nana requested me to pass the salt.
qa.e: A polite request uses requested/asked + object + to + verb.

qa.q: For which field did Rabindranath Tagore win the Nobel Prize in 1913?
qa.e: Tagore received the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1913.

qa.q: Which national song or anthem did Tagore write?
qa.e: Tagore wrote 'Jana Gana Mana', which is India's national anthem.

qa.q: Where did Tagore found Visva-Bharati?
qa.e: Visva-Bharati was founded by Tagore at Santiniketan in West Bengal.

qa.q: 'Yet when the evening kettle sings.' The kettle 'singing' is an example of:
qa.e: A kettle cannot really sing; giving it a human action is personification.

qa.q: 'Or jasmine scent drifts softly near.' Which sense does this line appeal to?
qa.e: 'Scent' is something we smell.

qa.q: What does 'nostalgic' mean?
qa.a: Full of tender longing for the past
qa.e: Being nostalgic means feeling a warm, slightly sad longing for past times.

qa.q: What does 'used to' show in 'Nani used to tell us stories every night'?
qa.a: A habit in the past that no longer happens
qa.e: 'Used to' + verb shows a regular past habit.

qa.q: 'She's far, yet always comes again.' What tone do these lines suggest?
qa.e: The speaker misses Nani but finds comfort that she 'comes again' in memory.

qa.q: What does 'inclusion' mean?
qa.a: Making sure everyone is welcomed and can take part
qa.e: Inclusion means no one is left out because of ability, background or any difference.

qa.q: A building is 'accessible' when:
qa.a: everyone, including people with disabilities, can reach and use it
qa.e: Accessible places can be reached and used by everyone, for example with ramps and lifts.

qa.q: What is 'empathy'?
qa.a: Understanding and sharing another person's feelings
qa.e: Empathy means putting yourself in someone else's place and feeling with them.

qa.q: Read: 'At the school pool, Nidhi swam a little slower than the others, so her coach gave her a lane of her own and timed her against her own best. By March she had beaten it three times.' What did the coach do?
qa.a: The coach set a fair challenge suited to Nidhi
qa.e: Timing Nidhi against her own best is a fair challenge that helped her improve.

qa.q: Choose the correct word: 'She ran ___ to the finish line.'
qa.e: The word describes how she ran (a verb), so we need the adverb 'quickly'.

qa.q: What is the opposite of 'include'?
qa.e: In- (in) and ex- (out) give the opposites include and exclude.

qa.q: Which is the most respectful way to describe someone?
qa.e: People-first language puts the person first and avoids pity or labels.

qa.q: Which word is a synonym of 'perseverance'?
qa.e: Perseverance and persistence both mean continuing to try despite difficulties.

qa.q: Special Olympics is a sports movement mainly for:
qa.e: Special Olympics was created to give people with intellectual disabilities the chance to train and compete.

qa.q: The oath says: 'Let me win. But if I cannot win, let me be brave in the attempt.' What does it value most?
qa.e: The oath values being brave and trying your best, even without a win.

qa.q: Who started the Special Olympics movement?
qa.e: Eunice Kennedy Shriver founded Special Olympics in the 1960s.

qa.q: What is the Special Olympics programme in India called?
qa.e: The programme in India is called Special Olympics Bharat.

qa.q: What are Unified Sports?
qa.a: Teams where people with and without intellectual disabilities play together
qa.e: Unified Sports put athletes with and without intellectual disabilities on the same team.

qa.q: Read: 'In the 50-metre race, Sana saw Joy trip near the start. She jogged back, helped him up, and they finished together, last but laughing. Their cheer was the loudest of the day.' Why was the cheer loudest for them?
qa.a: The crowd valued their kindness and friendship
qa.e: They finished last, so the cheer was for Sana's kindness and their spirit, not their speed.

qa.q: What does 'sportsmanship' mean?
qa.a: Fair and generous behaviour in sport
qa.e: Sportsmanship means playing fairly, respecting others and being gracious in winning or losing.

qa.q: Which phrase is correct?
qa.e: The natural collocation is 'take part in'.

qa.q: What is a narrative poem?
qa.a: A poem that tells a story
qa.e: A narrative poem tells a story with characters and events.

qa.q: 'We lost the match, the scoreboard said, / But all of us walked home ahead.' What is this an example of?
qa.e: Losing yet being 'ahead' seems contradictory, but it is true in spirit, so it is a paradox.

qa.q: 'The rival captain paused the play / And knelt to help her on her way.' What did the rival captain do?
qa.a: She stopped the game to help Meenu
qa.e: The lines say she paused the play and knelt to help Meenu.

qa.q: What is the theme of the original poem about Meenu?
qa.a: Kindness matters more than the score
qa.e: Even after losing, the team felt they were ahead because of the kindness shown.

qa.q: What is the climax of a story?
qa.a: The turning point or most intense moment
qa.e: The climax is the moment of greatest tension where the story turns.

qa.q: Which is a good rule for writing a summary?
qa.a: Include only the main points in your own words
qa.e: A summary is short, in your own words, and keeps only the main ideas.

qa.q: What is the simple past of 'kneel'?
qa.e: 'Knelt' is the usual past form of 'kneel'.

qa.q: In 'The rival captain paused the play', which word tells us the game stopped only for a short time?
qa.e: To pause is to stop for a short time before continuing.

qa.q: What is a melody?
qa.a: A tune made of a series of notes
qa.e: A melody is a sequence of notes heard as a tune.

qa.q: What does 'tempo' mean in music?
qa.e: Tempo is how fast or slow a piece of music is played.

qa.q: What are the 'lyrics' of a song?
qa.e: Lyrics are the words that are sung.

qa.q: In Indian classical music, what is a tala?
qa.e: A tala is a repeating cycle of beats; a raga is the melodic framework.

qa.q: M. S. Subbulakshmi, the first musician to receive the Bharat Ratna, was famous as a:
qa.e: M. S. Subbulakshmi was a celebrated Carnatic vocalist.

qa.q: The Carnatic tradition of classical music belongs mainly to which part of India?
qa.e: Carnatic music developed mainly in South India; Hindustani music mainly in the North.

qa.q: Which of these is a percussion instrument?
qa.e: The mridangam is a drum, played by striking, so it is percussion.

qa.q: Read: 'The power had gone out and the hostel was dark and silent. Then Tenzin began to strum his guitar. One by one, doors opened; someone tapped a steel plate, someone hummed along. By ten o'clock the corridor had become a concert hall.' What does the last sentence suggest?
qa.a: Everyone joined in and made music together
qa.e: It is figurative: so many people joined in that the corridor felt like a concert hall.

qa.q: 'Real friends stand by you in tough times.' What does 'stand by' mean here?
qa.e: 'Stand by someone' means to support them, especially in difficulty.

qa.q: Which phrasal verb means 'become friends again after a quarrel'?
qa.e: To make up is to end a quarrel and become friends again.

qa.q: What does 'A friend in need is a friend indeed' mean?
qa.a: A true friend helps you when you need it
qa.e: A real friend is one who helps when you are in trouble.

qa.q: Who is a 'confidant'?
qa.a: A person you trust with your secrets
qa.e: A confidant is someone you can confide in, that is, share secrets with.

qa.q: Choose the correct word: 'The girl ___ kite got stuck in the tree asked us for help.'
qa.e: The kite belongs to the girl, so we use the possessive 'whose'.

qa.q: What is the antonym of 'loyal'?
qa.e: Adding dis- gives the opposite: disloyal.

qa.q: 'After changing schools, the two friends slowly drifted apart.' What does 'drifted apart' mean?
qa.e: To drift apart is to slowly lose closeness over time, often without a fight.

qa.q: Read: 'Aditya and Faiz argued over a cricket bat in Class 5 and stopped speaking. Two years later, when Faiz broke his arm, Aditya carried his bag every day for a month. Soon they were inseparable again.' Which phrasal verb describes the ending?
qa.e: They became friends again, which is 'made up'. 'Fell out' describes the start.

qa.q: 'And taps my shoulder with its drums.' Music is given a human action here. Which device is this?
qa.e: Tapping someone's shoulder is a human action given to music.

qa.q: 'Dha-dhin, the tabla keeps the beat.' What is 'Dha-dhin' an example of?
qa.e: 'Dha-dhin' imitates the sound of the tabla.

qa.q: What is assonance?
qa.a: Repetition of vowel sounds inside nearby words
qa.e: Assonance repeats vowel sounds, as in 'sweet green leaves'.

qa.q: What is a refrain?
qa.a: A line or lines repeated in a poem or song
qa.e: A refrain is repeated, like a chorus.

qa.q: What is the central idea of the original poem 'When I am lonely, music comes...'?
qa.a: Music comforts the speaker like a friend
qa.e: Every instrument in the poem comforts the lonely speaker, like a friend.

qa.q: 'The flute-notes whisper, "Don't be blue."' What does 'blue' mean here?
qa.e: 'Feeling blue' is an idiom for feeling sad.

qa.q: In poetry, what is rhythm?
qa.a: The pattern of beats or stressed syllables
qa.e: Rhythm is the beat we hear when a poem is read aloud.

qa.q: Which line contains alliteration?
qa.e: 'Soft songs soothe ... soul' repeats the 's' sound at the start of words.

qa.q: Which of these is non-verbal communication?
qa.e: A namaste is a gesture; it communicates without words.

qa.q: Which sentence is most suitable for a letter to a municipal officer?
qa.a: I wish to draw your attention to the broken street lights in our colony.
qa.e: Formal letters use complete, polite sentences without slang.

qa.q: Which salutation is used in a formal letter to a principal?
qa.e: 'Sir' or 'Madam' (or 'Respected Sir/Madam') is the formal salutation.

qa.q: Which closing is used in a formal letter that begins with 'Sir'?
qa.e: A formal letter beginning 'Sir/Madam' traditionally ends with 'Yours faithfully'.

qa.q: What does PIN stand for in 'PIN code'?
qa.e: PIN stands for Postal Index Number, the six-digit code used by India Post.

qa.q: What is 'body language'?
qa.a: Communication through posture, gestures and expressions
qa.e: Body language is how our posture, gestures and expressions send messages.

qa.q: Read: 'Dadaji in the village cannot hear well on the phone, so Mitali writes him a postcard every month in big, clear letters. He keeps them all in a tin box and reads them aloud to visitors.' Why does Mitali write postcards?
qa.a: Because Dadaji cannot hear well on the phone
qa.e: The passage says he cannot hear well on the phone, so she chose writing.

qa.q: Which of these is a feature of informal writing?
qa.e: Contractions are common in friendly, informal writing; the others belong to formal letters.

qa.q: What is the connotation of a word?
qa.a: The feeling or idea it suggests beyond its basic meaning
qa.e: Connotation is the emotional shade a word carries, positive or negative.

qa.q: Which word describes someone careful with money in a positive way?
qa.e: 'Thrifty' praises careful spending; the others suggest meanness.

qa.q: Your friend's speech was too long. Which response is the kindest and most useful?
qa.a: Your opening was great; a shorter middle part would make it even better.
qa.e: It praises a real strength and gives a gentle, specific suggestion.

qa.q: Choose the correct word: '___ raining, so take an umbrella.'
qa.e: 'It's' is short for 'it is': It is raining.

qa.q: What is the denotation of a word?
qa.e: Denotation is the literal, dictionary meaning.

qa.q: What does 'The pen is mightier than the sword' mean?
qa.a: Words and ideas can be more powerful than force
qa.e: The saying means ideas and words can change the world more than violence can.

qa.q: Read: 'When Arnav forgot his lines on stage, a boy in the front row giggled. But his teacher whispered, "Take a breath; you know this." Arnav finished his speech and later said those words carried him through.' What does this show?
qa.a: Encouraging words can give a person strength
qa.e: The teacher's few kind words helped Arnav finish, showing the power of encouragement.

qa.q: Which word has a negative connotation?
qa.e: 'Nosy' suggests poking into others' business; the others sound positive or neutral.

qa.q: 'Words are seeds we gently sow.' Which device is used?
qa.e: Words are said to BE seeds, without 'like' or 'as', so it is a metaphor.

qa.q: What does 'A harsh word is a thorn that stings' mean?
qa.e: Like a thorn, a harsh word causes pain.

qa.q: What is the main message of the original poem 'Words are seeds we gently sow...'?
qa.a: Think carefully before you speak, because words last
qa.e: The poem says words grow in hearts and never die, so we must weigh them.

qa.q: In 'The light in the kitchen is on', what part of speech is 'light'?
qa.e: 'The light' names a thing, so it is a noun here.

qa.q: In 'She carried a light bag', what part of speech is 'light'?
qa.e: 'Light' describes the bag, so it is an adjective.

qa.q: Which word is the conjunction in 'I wanted to call, but my phone had no charge'?
qa.e: 'But' joins the two clauses and shows contrast.

qa.q: Which word is an adverb in 'He spoke softly to the baby'?
qa.e: 'Softly' tells how he spoke, so it is an adverb.

qa.q: What does 'weigh each word' mean in the poem?
qa.a: Think carefully about what you say
qa.e: To weigh words is to consider them carefully before speaking.

qa.q: What does 'aspire' mean?
qa.a: To hope and work to achieve something
qa.e: To aspire is to have a strong hope and to work towards it.

qa.q: Which word is a synonym of 'obstacle'?
qa.e: An obstacle is something in your way, like a hurdle.

qa.q: Choose the correct form: 'Watch out! That glass ___ fall off the edge.'
qa.e: We can see the glass about to fall, so we use 'is going to'.

qa.q: Choose the correct form: 'According to the timetable, the exam ___ at 10 a.m. on Monday.'
qa.e: The simple present is used for timetables and schedules.

qa.q: Read: 'At twelve, Neha dreamt of mountaineering, but she got breathless on the school stairs. She began with a walk around her colony each morning, then jogging, then weekend treks near Pune. Three years later, she reached a Himalayan base camp.' What does this show?
qa.a: Big goals can be reached through small, steady steps
qa.e: Neha moved from walks to jogs to treks, step by step, until she reached her goal.

qa.q: What was Kalpana Chawla's famous achievement?
qa.a: First woman of Indian origin to go to space
qa.e: Kalpana Chawla flew on the Space Shuttle and was the first woman of Indian origin in space.

qa.q: What is the noun form of 'ambitious'?
qa.e: 'Ambition' is the noun; 'ambitious' is the adjective.

qa.q: 'Passing the Grade 5 music exam was a milestone for Ishita.' What does 'milestone' mean here?
qa.e: Here 'milestone' is used figuratively for an important step forward.

qa.q: What is 'self-belief'?
qa.e: Self-belief means trusting that you can do something.

qa.q: What is the opposite of 'optimistic'?
qa.e: A pessimistic person expects bad outcomes, the opposite of optimistic.

qa.q: Which sentence correctly joins 'He was tired' and 'He kept practising' using 'although'?
qa.a: Although he was tired, he kept practising.
qa.e: 'Although' starts the first clause; we do not add 'but' as well.

qa.q: Which sentence is correct?
qa.e: 'Despite' is followed directly by a noun phrase: despite her injury.

qa.q: 'When the team needed one last goal, Arjun rose to the occasion.' What does this mean?
qa.a: He did well when it really mattered
qa.e: To rise to the occasion is to perform well at an important moment.

qa.q: 'Against all odds, the village team won the state title.' What does 'against all odds' mean?
qa.e: 'Against all odds' means succeeding even though success seemed very unlikely.

qa.q: Which is a positive self-talk version of 'I can't solve this'?
qa.a: I can't solve this yet, but I'll keep trying.
qa.e: Adding 'yet' and a plan to keep trying shows belief that you can improve.

qa.q: Read: 'Before the debate, Ira's hands were cold and her voice shook. She told herself, "I have practised; I am ready." She stepped up, took a deep breath and spoke clearly.' What helped Ira?
qa.e: Her positive self-talk about her practice gave her the confidence to speak.

qa.q: 'Believe the seed that dreams of tree, / Believe the stream that seeks the sea.' Which device does the repeated 'Believe' at the start of lines show?
qa.e: Repeating the same word at the beginning of lines is anaphora.

qa.q: What does 'The sky is not your ceiling' mean?
qa.a: There is no limit to what you can achieve
qa.e: A ceiling is an upper limit; the line says even the sky does not limit you.

qa.q: 'When storms say "Stop!" and doubts say "No"'. Storms and doubts speaking is an example of:
qa.e: Speaking is a human action given to storms and doubts.

qa.q: Which of these is an imperative sentence?
qa.e: It begins with a base verb and gives encouragement, with 'you' understood.

qa.q: What is the subject of an imperative sentence like 'Stand firm'?
qa.e: In imperatives the subject 'you' is understood, not written.

qa.q: In which person is a diary entry usually written?
qa.e: A diary records your own experiences, so it uses 'I'.

qa.q: What is the central idea of the original poem 'Believe the seed that dreams of tree...'?
qa.a: Trust yourself and keep going despite doubts
qa.e: The poem urges us to believe, stand firm and go on, because there is no limit.

qa.q: Which sentence is exclamatory?
qa.a: What a brave climber she is!
qa.e: It expresses strong feeling with 'What' and an exclamation mark.
